unit.can_do_en: make a shopping list and follow a simple recipe.

brief.situation_en: Aino visits Maria. They plan dinner.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: What shall we make for dinner?

judge.reason: Same question about what we are making for food; only register differs (tehään/teemme, ruuaks/ruoaksi).

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Salmon soup! I'm learning Finnish food.

judge.reason: Same: salmon soup, I am learning Finnish food; only register differences.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: Good idea. What do we need?

judge.reason: Same: good idea, what do we need; tarvitaan/tarvitsemme is register.
Same question: do we have onion; onks/onko, meil/meillä, sipulii/sipulia are register.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: No. Write it on the list.

judge.reason: Same: we don't have any; write it on the list. Only register differences.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: OK. Let's go to the shop!

judge.reason: Okei and Selvä are both 'OK'; same suggestion to go to the store.

forms.why_en: The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Me means we. People say it the same way.
Books write teemme. Speech says me tehään, the same form as 'one does', for 'we do'.
Adds -ksi for 'as' or 'for': ruoka becomes ruoaksi. Speech says ruuaks.
The partitive singular is used for some soup: lohikeitto becomes lohikeittoa. Speech says lohikeittoo.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Opetella, to learn, with -n for 'I': opettelen.
Suomalainen changes to suomalaista to match ruokaa: suomalaista ruokaa, 'Finnish food'.
Adds -a for food in general: ruoka becomes ruokaa.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Books write me tarvitsemme. Speech says me tarvitaan, the same form as 'one needs', for 'we need'.
Lohi becomes lohta for some salmon: the i drops and -ta is added.
Plural 'some' takes -ita: peruna becomes perunoita, the last a turning into o.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Plural 'some' takes -ita: porkkana becomes porkkanoita, the last a turning into o.
The partitive singular is used for some cream: kerma becomes kermaa.
Adds -ä for some dill: tilli becomes tilliä.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Me takes -llä for 'has': meillä on, 'we have'. Speech shortens -llä to -l: meillä becomes meil.
Adds -a for some onion: sipuli becomes sipulia. Speech turns the a into i: sipulii.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
After ei the verb drops its ending: olla becomes ole. Speech shortens ole to oo.
The imperative for one person drops the ending: kirjoittaa becomes kirjoita. Speech says kirjota.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -an for 'into': lista becomes listaan. You write it into the list.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
The passive form means 'let's' here: mennään, let's go.
Adds -an for 'to': kauppa becomes kauppaan.
